lines: Two engineers sit down to benchmark the exact same query, on the exact same database.
They come back with numbers that are twice as far apart as the real gap between an ordinary day and a genuinely bad one.
One of them started measuring the instant the service came up. The other one waited a few minutes before touching anything.
So who actually got closer to the truth here, and what changed in those few quiet minutes of waiting.
Think about everything a freshly started service hasn't done yet.
answer: The one who waited was closer, and nothing about the first engineer's method was carelessly wrong.
An empty buffer pool and an empty cache were still quietly absorbing most of those early, slow requests. Waiting let both of them fill in before anything got measured for real.

lines: Here's the honest list of reasons the first few minutes of almost any benchmark lie to you.

A compiler still warming itself up, a buffer pool and a page cache starting out completely empty, caches that haven't been asked a single question yet, background cleanup work piling up unseen, and small files that haven't had time to accumulate.
This sandbox's own database happens to reproduce exactly two of those five causes for real.
Restarting the database empties both its own buffer pool and the operating system's cache sitting underneath it.
Run the shop's ordinary order lookup immediately after that restart, and the very first handful of requests come back measurably slower than anything that follows.
Watch a sliding window of recent request times, and compare its average to the window that came right before it.
Once that change settles down and stays small for several windows running, steady state gets declared, not guessed at.
A single steady state run still carries real sampling noise hiding inside it.
Repeat that same run several separate times, and report a confidence interval around the result, so a reader can actually tell a true difference apart from ordinary noise.
That same query's cold start number and its steady state number are honestly answering two different real questions.

One is what a service that restarts constantly actually sees. The other is what a service that stays up for days sees. Blending the two together into one average answers neither question anyone actually asked.
Pulling this together now.

The first minutes of a benchmark lie for named, reproducible reasons. Steady state gets detected from the data, never just assumed. Repeated runs earn themselves a confidence interval instead of a single lonely number.
And cold cache and hot cache stay two separate, honestly labeled results, never folded into one blended figure.
A vendor hands you a single benchmark number, with no mention anywhere of warm up or how many times it was run.
What would you actually ask before trusting that number at all.
answer: Ask plainly whether warm up was ever discarded, and whether the run was repeated more than once.
Without both of those, that number is very likely still measuring the system waking up, not the system actually running.
An accurate number from a run like that still isn't telling you what you think it's telling you.
